title: The Avadhuta's Lessons from the Elements
story:
"The earth taught me forbearance," the avadhuta said. "Every being walks upon her — beasts and men, armies in their thousands, the hooves of cattle, the wheels of carts. She is trampled by all of them, morning and evening, and she never once strays from her course. So the wise one, though the world treads on him, does not leave his path."

He had been wronged a hundred times, Yadu thought — by rivals, by fate, by his own temper — and he had never once stayed on the path because of it; he had veered off it in fury. The first lesson had already found its mark.

"The wind taught me detachment," the avadhuta said. "It moves everywhere — through palaces and market streets, through the trees, into every corner of every house — and it clings to nothing it touches. So the yogi moves among the objects of the senses and remains unattached, passing through the world without being caught by it."

The wind, the king realized, had taught this man what he had spent his life failing to learn: to be in the middle of things and not be caught by them.

"The sky taught me to remain unaffected. The clouds sail through it, the rain falls from it, the smoke of a thousand hearths rises into it, the birds cross it — and none of them leaves a mark. In the same way the wise one dwells among all the bodies of the world, moving and unmoving, hidden in each one and touched by none; the sky is everywhere, and nowhere is it held, and so he sees the one self in all things and knows himself in everything."

"The water taught me purity. It is clear by nature and sweet to the taste, and wherever it flows it becomes a holy place — a tirtha for men to bathe in. So the sage, pure in himself, makes everything around him sacred; people come to him as they come to a river, and the dirt they carry falls from them in his presence."

"The fire taught me to be untainted. Whatever it is given — wood, refuse, offerings, filth — it burns, and takes no stain from any of it. It shines by its own heat; it is brilliant, and hard to approach. So the sage, whatever he consumes, is not polluted by it. His light is his own, and the world's dirt does not reach it."

"The moon taught me to wax and to wane. It swells to fullness and thins to a sliver, and both are its own nature. So the body rises and falls — birth, youth, age, death, all the states from the first to the cremation ground — and these belong to the body, not to the self. The wise one watches them as the moon watches its own phases, taking what time brings and letting it go when time takes it."

"The sun taught me the one soul in many bodies. One sun rises on the palace and on the hut, on the king and on the beggar, and illumines them all. So the one self appears in every body, and when a body ends, nothing of the light is lost; the wise one lives in that single sight, seeing himself in every face."

The king was silent. Seven lessons, each one drawn from a thing that had never spoken a word — and each one clear as water. He had filled his court with the learned, and none of them had ever told him anything so simply. The avadhuta paused, and when the king leaned forward, he went on — to the eighth of his teachers, the pigeon, and to what love had cost it.
reflection: The seven elemental lessons are striking because each is drawn from a teacher that never spoke: forbearance from the trampled earth, detachment from the wind, purity from water, radiance that takes no stain from fire. And the sun's lesson gathers them all — the one self in many bodies — showing that the elements were never teaching about themselves, but about the single reality reflected in all of them.

hero_scene: On the forest road, the ragged avadhuta sits cross-legged with one hand raised, counting off his teachers — earth, wind, sky, water, fire, moon, sun — while King Yadu listens on the ground before him, the evening sky turning behind them.

King Yadu seated before him, listening
the earth, wind, sky, water, fire, moon and sun rendered as small visions above the sage
the evening forest road, quiet and golden
